subject: Banking
title: SPACs and Blank Check Companies
description: A micro-lesson that makes SPACs and Blank Check Companies usable.

hook.text: A SPAC raises money through an IPO with no business. It is a blank check company that promises to buy something later.

buildup.text: In 2021, SPACs raised $162 billion. Companies used them to go public faster.

discovery.text: SPAC sponsors earn 20% of shares for free, called the promote.

twist.text: By 2023, most SPAC mergers had destroyed value. The average SPAC stock dropped 50% or more after the deal closed.

climax.text: SPACs were a loophole around IPO rules that mostly benefited sponsors.

punchline.text: $162 billion raised, most lost. SPACs enriched sponsors, not investors.

quiz.question: What is the SPAC sponsor's 'promote'?
options: A free 20% stake in the company for organizing the deal

details.summary: A SPAC is a shell company that raises money through an IPO with no existing business, then uses the funds to acquire a private company within two years, offering that company a faster alternative path to going public.
details.whyItMatters: SPACs exploded in popularity during 2020-2021, raising over 250 billion dollars. The subsequent crash and regulatory crackdown revealed how the structure often enriched sponsors while leaving public investors with losses.
takeaways: SPACs go public first and find an acquisition target afterward
SPAC sponsors receive 20 percent of shares as a promote, diluting investors
Most SPACs that completed mergers have underperformed the market

faq.question: Why would a company choose a SPAC over a traditional IPO?
faq.answer: SPACs allow companies to go public faster with more certainty on pricing. Unlike traditional IPOs, SPAC targets can make forward-looking financial projections in their marketing, which is restricted in regular IPOs.

faq.question: Why did most SPAC investments lose money?
faq.answer: The sponsor promote dilutes investor value by 20 percent from day one. Many SPAC targets were low-quality companies that could not have gone public through traditional IPOs. Overly optimistic projections rarely materialized.
